candidates.quote: The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is.
candidates.author: Marcel Proust
candidates.locator: chapter 2, the Vinteuil septet passage (trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff, 1929)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence behind the paraphrase Calendar For Life carries, and the real one says the thing itself: to see through the eyes of another is the only voyage worth making.

candidates.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things can not be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.
candidates.author: Mark Twain
candidates.whyThisMonth: The second sentence is the one that earns the month: the goal of going out among strangers is charitable views of them.

candidates.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
candidates.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
candidates.locator: Part I, In the Valley, chapter IV, The Scot Abroad (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Nobody you meet today is foreign; the strangeness travels with you, which is a gentle way to start widening the circle.

candidates.quote: Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
candidates.author: Ian Fleming
candidates.locator: chapter 20, The Nature of Evil (Jonathan Cape, 1953) (René Mathis)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A friend telling a cold man to put people before abstractions: the plainest morning case for kindness in the whole list.
candidates.speaker: René Mathis

candidates.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Others were here before you and others will come after: the line that makes a comfortable person look past the fence.
candidates.speaker: Gildor Inglorion

candidates.quote: If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: chapter 18, The Return Journey (George Allen and Unwin, 1937) (Thorin Oakenshield)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A proud man’s last word is that cheer shared beats gold kept, and the line stands on its own without the deathbed around it.
candidates.speaker: Thorin Oakenshield

candidates.author: Albert Camus
candidates.locator: Part One, The Rebel (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Camus turns the cogito outward: the first thing a protest proves is that other people are real, and it founds its value on the whole human race.

candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.whyThisMonth: Kindness in practice, from the one woman in this lane: feed people properly before you ask them to think or to love.
